results.content: Wei and Carroll (2009) took an iterative approach that assumed linearity of the quantile functions and provided an approach based on estimating equations to fit quantile regression models with a scalar-valued covariate affected by measurement error. The steps in SIMEX are as follows: (i) simulate additional measurement errors with increasing variances and add them to the observed data, ; (ii) obtain regression coefficient estimates from the model of interest using the simulated data prone to errors; (iii) repeat the simulation and estimation steps a large number of times; (iv) obtain the averaged values of the estimates to be used to determine the relationship between the measurement-error-induced bias and the variance of the errors; and (v) extrapolate the relationship back to the case of no measurement error, (see Carroll *and others*, 2006; Cook and Stefanski, 1994; Stefanski and Cook, 1995; Carroll and Stefanski, 1997; Mao and Wei, 2017, for details).

results.title: Extrapolation for Time-Series and Cross-Sectional Data
results.content: To make extrapolations: • Combine estimates of the level; • Use a simple representation of trend unless there is strong evidence to the contrary; • Weight the most recent data more heavily than earlier data when measurement errors are small, forecast horizons are short, and the series is stable; • Be conservative when the situation is uncertain; • Use domain knowledge to provide pre-specified adjustments to extrapolations; • Use statistical procedures as an aid in selecting an extrapolation method; • Update estimates of model parameters frequently; and • Use cycles only when the evidence on future timing and amplitude is highly accurate.

results.title: Measurement error correction methods for the effects of ambient air pollution on mortality and morbidity using the UK Biobank cohort: the MELONS study - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Measurement error correction methods for the effects of ambient air pollution on mortality and morbidity using the UK Biobank cohort: the MELONS study. Measurement error-corrected effect estimates were larger than uncorrected estimates. Data from an existing personal monitoring campaign was used as an external validation dataset to estimate measurement error structures between “true” personal exposure and several surrogate (measured and modelled) estimates of assigned exposure, allowing for the application of two health effect estimate correction methodologies: regression calibration (RCAL) and simulation extrapolation (SIMEX). Uncorrected hazard ratios (HRs) suggested an increase in the risk of natural-cause mortality for modelled NO2 estimates (HR: 1.028 [0.983, 1.074] per IQR increment of 14.54 μg/m3) and no statistically significant association was observed for PM2.5 surrogate exposure measures. Measurement error corrected HRs were generally larger in magnitude, although exhibited wider confidence intervals than uncorrected effect estimates. These findings suggest that health effect estimates not corrected for exposure measurement error may lead to underestimation in the magnitude of effects.

results.title: Parameter Estimation for Differential Equation Models Using a Framework of Measurement Error in Regression Models - PMC
results.content: In this paper, we propose parameter estimation methods for ordinary differential equation models (ODE) based on the local smoothing approach and a pseudo-least squares (PsLS) principle under a framework of measurement error in regression models. To estimate the parameters of interest in the ODE model (1.1) under the framework of measurement errors in a nonlinear regression model, we first need to estimate the state variable **X**(*t*) and its derivative **X**′(*t*). Note that in this objective function, {*X̂*(*ti*), *X̂*′(*ti*); *i* = 1, …, *n*} are not the observed data and measured covariates, instead they are the smoothing estimates of the state variable *X*(*t*) and its derivative which are not independently distributed. We applied the proposed PsLS and SIMEX methods to the simulated data sets to estimate the unknown parameters (*α*, *β*, *γ*) in the FitzHugh-Nagumo equations. We present the predicted curves of *X*1(*t*) and *X*2(*t*) and their derivatives for the case of from the two methods, PsLS and SIMEX, as well as the corresponding true curves (by solving the ODEs using the true parameter values) in Figure 1, in which the associated 95% pointwise confidence intervals, i.e., the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the estimates from the 500 replications, of these state variables and their derivatives are also delineated. Formal statistical estimation methods for parameters in ordinary differential equation (ODE) models are relatively new in statistical literature (Li et al., 2002; Huang and Wu, 2006; Huang, Liu and Wu, 2006; Ramsay et al., 2007; Chen and Wu 2008a, 2008b; Miao et al. 2007) in the sense of estimation efficiency or accuracy, but instead our method provides an alternative estimation approach for ODE models in the framework of measurement error models to avoid some critical problems of these existing methods that include: i) the requirement and sensitivity of initial values of the state variables for ordinary differential equation (ODE) models on the parameter estimation, in particular for the NLS method; ii) the convergence problem of the NLS method and other existing methods; iii) high computational cost due to iteratively solving the ODEs numerically in the estimation procedure; and iv) high computational cost due to complicated optimization techniques.

results.title: Generalizability Theory (G Theory): Complete Guide to Measurement Reliability | Cogn-IQ
results.content: Generalizability Theory is a statistical framework that extends classical test theory by simultaneously considering multiple sources of measurement error. Developed by Cronbach and colleagues in the 1960s-1970s, it uses variance components analysis to partition observed score variance into effects from different facets (sources of variation) and their interactions. * Distinguishes between G studies (variance components) and D studies (decision making). Generalizability Theory (G Theory) represents a major advancement in psychometric theory, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding and quantifying measurement error. Unlike Classical Test Theory (CTT), which considers only a single, undifferentiated source of error, G Theory recognizes that measurement error arises from multiple sources and provides methods to identify, estimate, and minimize these various error components. Developed by Lee Cronbach, Goldine Gleser, Nanda Rajaratnam, and colleagues during the 1960s and 1970s, G Theory emerged from the recognition that test scores are influenced by numerous factors beyond the attribute being measured. * Apply G Theory principles to improve measurement design. In G Theory, facets are the various conditions or dimensions that can affect measurement outcomes. The theory allows researchers to examine how each facet and their interactions contribute to the total variance in scores. G Theory conceptualizes measurement within a universe of admissible observations—all possible acceptable measurement conditions. Common Variance Components in G Theory. A G study is designed to estimate variance components associated with different facets and their interactions. The G study answers questions about the relative magnitude of different sources of measurement error and identifies which facets contribute most substantially to score variability. A D study uses variance component estimates from the G study to evaluate different measurement designs and make practical decisions about test construction. G Theory is extensively used in educational measurement to optimize test designs and scoring procedures. The theory can identify whether measurement error primarily stems from task sampling, rater disagreement, or person-by-task interactions, guiding improvements in assessment design. Survey researchers apply G Theory to evaluate measurement quality when multiple interviewers collect data across different locations and time periods. The framework allows researchers to evaluate multiple reliability questions within a single study and to predict reliability for different measurement designs without collecting additional data.
